analysis.one_liner: Suspends royalty subsidies for oil and gas companies drilling on federal lands when prices are high.
analysis.headline: The bill to end high-price royalty relief for federal-land oil and gas drilling never left committee and died without a vote at the end of the 109th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Some oil and gas companies drill on federal land and offshore areas under leases that let them skip paying royalties — a share of the value of what they pump — when Congress intended to encourage production. This bill would switch that off whenever oil topped about $35 a barrel or natural gas prices were similarly high, meaning companies would pay the government royalties in good times. It would also have required the Interior Department to renegotiate existing leases to the same effect, and to deny new leases to companies that refused.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would collect royalty payments from oil and gas produced on public land during periods of high prices, and ordinary consumers whose taxes subsidize drilling that is profitable anyway.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Interior Secretary to suspend any royalty relief whenever average crude oil prices exceed $34.71 per barrel or natural gas wellhead prices exceed $4.34 per thousand cubic feet over a four-week period [S3].

It requires the Secretary to seek to renegotiate existing federal leases so that royalty relief does not apply during high-price periods, and bars companies that refuse to renegotiate from obtaining new federal leases [S3].
The CRS summary describes the bill as requiring payment of royalties to the federal government for oil and gas production from federal lands when prices exceed specified thresholds [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases, who would pay royalties during high-price periods and could lose access to new federal leases if they refused to renegotiate older ones.

drawbacks.text: The bill would modify the terms of existing leases after they were signed, which oil companies and some legal observers would argue breaks negotiated contract terms and could invite litigation; Congress instead conditioned future lease eligibility on renegotiation to reach the same end [S3].

The price triggers are fixed in the bill — about $35 per barrel of oil — so the relief ends at prices well below where they actually traded in 2006, and critics could argue that removing price-based incentives might discourage production on federal lands when energy costs to consumers are already high [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is simple: companies would give up a subsidy that only matters when prices are already high, and the public would collect the royalties. The main honest objection is legal — rewriting signed leases raises contract-rights questions — but the bill tries to thread this by making renegotiation voluntary and new-lease access conditional, which slows enforcement rather than forcing compensation. On balance it is a taxpayer-recovery bill whose costs fall on a concentrated, profitable industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee the week it was introduced, no hearing or vote ever happened, and the bill expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the bill on February 14, 2006, and it was referred to the House Committee on Resources the same day [S5].

On February 17, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and executive comment was requested from the Interior Department; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the Senate, and the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases kept their price-based royalty relief for the remainder of the 109th Congress, and federal taxpayers went on forgoing royalty payments during high-price periods. The committee with jurisdiction faced no vote and no recorded position.

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on February 14, 2006 [S5].

for.name: 31 cosponsors (30 House Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 31 backers including members like Mrs. Maloney, Mr. Waxman, and Mr. Emanuel who joined as original introducers [S4].

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee (Chair Richard Pombo)
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; chaired by Rep. Richard Pombo (R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on February 14, 2006 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the record shows no committee action beyond assignment to a subcommittee [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent; the bill sat in a Republican-controlled committee and never advanced, with no Republican sponsor or floor vote ever recorded [S4].

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal lands and offshore leases
industries.note: The bill ends their price-triggered royalty waivers during high-price periods and conditions future federal leases on renegotiating old ones. Their gain under the status quo — pumping public resources while forgoing royalty payments when prices spike — comes directly out of federal revenue that ordinary taxpayers otherwise receive [S3].
